Three takes. I assumed the calendar invite is yours to move and that 9:45 is local team time.

**Take A, flat.**
> Standup moves to 9:45 starting Monday. Same link, same channel. Invite is updated.

**Take B, gives the reason.**
> Heads up: standup shifts to 9:45 from Monday, so the folks on the east side of the map aren't dialing in half-asleep. Same link. Calendar's already updated.

**Take C, shortest.**
> Standup is 9:45 from Monday. Invite updated.

Take A. It answers what, when, and "do I need to do anything" in three lines, and the reason in B invites a debate about the reason. If someone asks why, tell them then.

Swap the reason in B for the real one if you use it. I made that one up.

The specifics below are invented, since you didn't give me the cache details. Replace the commit hash, the key description, and the TTL with the real ones, or tell me what actually broke and I'll rewrite it.

```
Revert "Cache project list responses"

This reverts commit <sha>.

The cache key didn't include anything that changes on write, so
renames and deletes kept serving the pre-write payload until the
TTL expired. Users saw stale project lists for up to <ttl> after
their own edits.

Reverting to get correctness back. Re-landing needs invalidation
on the write path first, not a shorter TTL.
```

The last line is the part worth keeping whatever else you change. Without it the next person re-lands the same change with a 30-second TTL and ships the same bug, just harder to reproduce.

`<Name>` fields and the reason for the intro are placeholders. The second sentence is the one that matters, so make the "because" specific to what they're each doing, otherwise it reads as a networking chore and both of them will slow-walk it.

**Subject:** `<Ana>` <> `<Ben>`

> `<Ana>`, meet `<Ben>`, who owns `<billing infra>` and has been fighting the same `<double-charge>` problem you hit last month. `<Ben>`, `<Ana>`'s team already built `<the idempotency-key layer>` for `<checkout>`, so it's worth 30 minutes before either of you builds it twice.

Alternate second sentence if there's no concrete overlap yet:

> You two are the only people here who've shipped `<X>` at this size, and you've never talked, which seems like a waste. I'll leave it with you.

Version number, date, and the timezone specifics are placeholders. I assumed Keep a Changelog format since that's what most repos land on. Tell me if yours is user-facing release notes instead and I'll drop the section headers and rewrite it in plain sentences.

```markdown
## [<1.8.0>] - <2026-08-19>

### Added
- **CSV export** for `<reports>`. Export runs against the current filter set,
  not the full table, so what you see is what you get. Files over `<50k rows>`
  are emailed rather than downloaded inline.

### Fixed
- Timestamps were rendered in `<UTC>` regardless of the account timezone,
  so anything logged after `<17:00>` local showed on the following day.
  Now rendered in the account timezone. Historical data is unaffected;
  only the display was wrong.
```

The "historical data is unaffected" line is the one to check before you publish. If the bug wrote bad values into storage rather than just displaying them wrong, that's a different entry and it needs a migration note.

Three takes, differing in how much they assume about the user. All of them put a create action in the copy, since an empty state without one is just a shrug.

**Take A, neutral.**
> **No projects yet**
> Projects hold your `<work, files, and collaborators>` in one place.
> `[ Create a project ]`

**Take B, action-first, no preamble.**
> **Start your first project**
> You'll be able to invite people and `<import existing files>` once it exists.
> `[ Create a project ]`

**Take C, for users who probably arrived by invite.**
> **Nothing here yet**
> Projects you create or get invited to will show up here.
> `[ Create a project ]`

Take B for a fresh signup. Take C if this list is also what an invited teammate sees before anyone adds them, because telling that person to "start your first project" is wrong and mildly alarming.

Pick based on which one your routing actually produces. If both users hit the same screen, use C and put the create button as the primary action anyway.

Every number below except the 40 minutes is a placeholder, including revenue, order counts, and the certificate's owner. Fill them from the real data before this circulates; a postmortem with invented impact figures is worse than one with blanks.

## Summary

Checkout was unavailable for 40 minutes on `<2026-08-14, 14:12 to 14:52 UTC>` because the TLS certificate for `<payments-gateway.internal>` expired. Every checkout request failed at the TLS handshake, so no orders could be completed for the duration. `<N>` checkout attempts failed and `<$X>` in orders were not captured. `<M>` of those customers returned and completed a purchase within 24 hours; the rest we assume are lost.

The certificate was issued manually in `<2025>` with a `<one-year>` lifetime and was never added to the automated renewal set. The expiry monitor covers certificates registered in `<cert-manager>` and this one was not, so nothing alerted before it expired. We found out from the checkout error-rate alarm, which fired `<4>` minutes after the failures started.

Recovery was a manual reissue and deploy, `<31>` minutes from page to resolution. Detection was fast; the delay was in finding which certificate had expired, because the gateway logged a generic handshake failure and not the subject or expiry date.

**Contributing factors:** a manually issued certificate outside the automated renewal path, no inventory reconciling issued certificates against monitored ones, and an upstream error message that didn't name the failing certificate.

**Not a factor:** the `<July>` gateway deploy. It was the first suspect during the incident and cost us `<8>` minutes of the response. It touched routing, not TLS material.

The interesting part isn't the expired certificate, it's that we had no list of certificates that renewal doesn't cover. That gap is still open for anything else issued by hand, and we don't currently know what else is on that list. Action items follow in the next section.

Two takes. Company name, stack, and location are placeholders, and the "first" framing only works if it's genuinely the first, so check that before posting.

**Take A, describes the job.**
> We're hiring our first design engineer at `<Company>`.
>
> That means one person owning the whole path from "this interaction feels wrong" to the merged PR that fixes it. Not a designer who hands off, not a frontend engineer who implements someone else's file. Both halves, same person, same day.
>
> It's the first hire of its kind here, so you'd be setting how the role works rather than inheriting it. `<Remote in EU>` or `<London>`. Details and application: `<link>`

**Take B, leads with the problem.**
> Our product works and doesn't feel like anything.
>
> So we're hiring our first design engineer: someone who can hold taste and a code editor at the same time, and who gets annoyed by the 200ms of jank the rest of us have learned to ignore.
>
> First one here, so you'd define the role. `<Remote in EU>` or `<London>`. `<link>`

Take B. "We're hiring" posts are wallpaper, and the first line of B is the only part of either that a person scrolling would stop for. It costs you a small public admission that the product isn't beautiful yet, which is the trade.

If your leadership won't sign off on that first line, take A works fine; just don't dilute B into A by editing it halfway.

Three takes, differing mainly in how much of an out you give them. I assumed you have some idea whether the reviewer is swamped or has just lost the thread.

**Take A, plain ask.**
> Hey `<name>`, `<PR #412>` has been open since Tuesday and it's blocking `<the export work>`. Any chance of a look today? If you're buried, tell me and I'll find another reviewer.

**Take B, when it's small.**
> `<PR #412>` is still waiting, `<80 lines>`, mostly deletions. Ten minutes if you have them today.

**Take C, when they've said yes and not done it.**
> Still need eyes on `<PR #412>`. It's three days old and `<the export work>` is stacked behind it. If today doesn't work, say so and I'll reassign it, no hard feelings.

Take A. The offer to reassign is the part that does the work: it turns "please do this" into a decision they can close in one word, and people answer decisions faster than requests.

Say what it's blocking. A nudge without a cost attached is easy to file under "later", and three days is already later.

Instrument the pipeline before you optimize any of it. Everyone on your team has a theory about which stage is slow and in my experience the theories are wrong about half the time, usually because the loud stage is not the long one.

## Get the numbers

1. **Emit a timestamp at every stage boundary.** Most CI systems already record per-step duration; if yours does, you're mostly done. If it's a shell script, wrap each phase and log epoch seconds to a file you collect at the end.
2. **Collect 10 to 20 real deploys**, not one. A single run tells you nothing about variance, and variance is often the actual complaint. A deploy that takes 25 minutes every time is annoying; one that takes 8 to 40 is what people dread.
3. **Sort stages by total time and by variance separately.** Two different lists, two different fixes.

## What you'll almost certainly find

The usual suspects, roughly in order of how often they turn out to be the bulk of it:

- **Dependency installation** with a cold or ineffective cache. Check whether your cache key actually hits. A cache that misses every run looks like a cache in the config and behaves like no cache at all.
- **Serial stages that don't depend on each other.** Lint, unit tests, and image build often run in sequence for no reason beyond the order someone wrote them in.
- **A full test suite gating deploy**, including slow integration tests that could run post-merge instead.
- **Waiting.** Queue time for a runner, waiting for a health check with a fixed sleep, a rollout that waits on a conservative readiness probe. This one hides from per-step timing if you only measure your own scripts, so measure wall clock from trigger to done and subtract the sum of your stages. The gap is queue and wait.

## The call

Fix variance before you fix the mean. Predictable-and-slow is a scheduling problem people work around; unpredictable is what makes them dread it. Then take the single largest stage and either cache it, parallelize it, or move it out of the deploy path.

One thing to decide, not me: whether some tests move to post-deploy with a fast rollback instead of gating. That trades a bit of risk for a lot of minutes, and it depends on how good your rollback actually is. If you can't roll back in under two minutes, don't make that trade yet.

Turn it on, but not repo-wide in one commit. That version is the trap, not strict mode itself.

The flag people mean by "strict" is really seven flags, and `strictNullChecks` accounts for the overwhelming majority of new errors in an old codebase. The others are comparatively cheap.

## How to do it without a two-month branch

1. **Turn on the cheap flags first**, repo-wide: `noImplicitThis`, `alwaysStrict`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictFunctionTypes`. These usually produce error counts in the dozens, not thousands.
2. **Measure `strictNullChecks` before committing to it.** Flip it locally, run `tsc --noEmit`, count. That number decides your approach and takes ten minutes to get.
3. **If the count is large, go file-by-file.** Set `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json` and list the not-yet-clean files in `exclude`, or use the inverse approach with `ts-strict-plugin` style per-file opt-in comments. Either way you get a shrinking list, which is a thing a team can actually finish.
4. **Make new files strict from day one.** This is where most of the value is. It stops the pile growing while you dig at it.
5. **Convert files when you're already in them** for other reasons. Do not staff a dedicated migration.

## The part worth flagging

`strictNullChecks` will find real bugs, and some of them are in code that currently works by accident. Expect a few "fixes" that change runtime behavior. Review those as behavior changes, not type changes, or you will ship a regression inside a PR that everyone rubber-stamps because it's "just types."

Also resist `as` and `!` as the migration tool. If a third of the diff is non-null assertions you've bought the error count down without buying any safety, and now the codebase claims a guarantee it doesn't have. That's worse than staying loose, because it's misleading.

## My position

Do it. The incremental path costs you close to nothing and the alternative is that the codebase gets bigger and the flip gets more expensive every quarter. The only case for skipping is a codebase you're actively planning to retire within a year.

A cache is a second copy of your data that is allowed to be wrong for a while, and every strategy is just a different answer to "how long, and who fixes it."

That's the whole mental shift from working with a database directly. The database is the truth. The cache is a faster copy that has no idea when the truth changed. Everything below is a scheme for telling it.

## The four you'll actually encounter

**TTL, or time to live.** You stamp the cached copy with an expiry: 60 seconds, an hour. When it expires, the next read goes back to the database and refills it. Nobody has to notify anybody. The cost is that for up to one TTL, you serve data you know might be stale. This is the right default far more often than people admit, and it's the only strategy that can't develop a correctness bug, because being stale is the documented behavior rather than a failure.

**Write-through.** Every write goes to the database and the cache in the same operation. The cache is never stale because it's updated in lockstep. The catch is that you now have two systems in one write path, so you need an answer for what happens when the database write succeeds and the cache write fails. Usually the answer is "delete the cache entry and let the next read refill it," which means you've quietly turned it into the next strategy.

**Write-invalidate, or cache-aside with deletion.** Reads check the cache, fall back to the database on a miss, and store the result. Writes go to the database and then *delete* the cached entry rather than updating it. The next read refills it from truth. This is the most common production pattern and the one to reach for first. The failure mode is that you forget one write path, and then that one path serves stale data forever while everything else works. Which is why the third question below matters.

**Versioned or content-addressed keys.** Instead of invalidating, you change the key. Cache under `user:123:v7`, and when the user changes, bump to `v8`. The old entry is now unreachable and expires on its own. Nothing needs deleting, so nothing can be missed. Costs you memory holding garbage until it ages out, and requires a cheap way to know the current version.

## The three questions that pick one for you

1. **How wrong can this be, in seconds, before someone is harmed?** A homepage article list, minutes. An account balance, zero. The answer to "zero" is often "don't cache it."
2. **How many code paths write this data?** One service and one function, invalidation is easy. Six services, three cron jobs, and a manual admin tool, invalidation will be missed and TTL is safer because it's self-healing.
3. **What happens on a cache miss storm?** If the entry expires and a thousand requests all miss at once, they all hit the database simultaneously. This is a stampede, and it takes down more systems than staleness does. The fix is a short lock so one request refills while others wait or serve the stale copy.

## Where to start

Cache-aside with deletion on writes, plus a TTL as a backstop even though you've got invalidation. The TTL costs you nothing and it means a missed invalidation is a bug that lasts an hour instead of forever. Belt and braces here is not paranoia, it's the difference between a bug you notice in staging and one a customer reports in six months.

Cut the pages before you touch the rotation. Six people is a workable rotation size; it becomes unworkable when the pages are noisy, and rearranging the schedule around noise just moves the pain to a different person.

Get the last 90 days of pages and sort every one into three buckets:

- **Real, and action was required.** Something was broken and a human had to intervene.
- **Real, but self-resolved** before or shortly after someone looked. Transient, retried, cleared on its own.
- **Not real.** Threshold too tight, flapping check, alert on a symptom nobody acts on.

On most teams I've seen do this, the first bucket is under a quarter of the total. If yours matches, your on-call problem is an alerting problem wearing a scheduling costume.

## What to change, in order

1. **Delete every alert in bucket three this week.** Not tune, delete. You can re-add one if something is missed. An alert nobody acts on trains people to ignore the ones that matter, which is the real damage.
2. **For bucket two, raise the threshold or add a delay** so the system gets a chance to fix itself before waking anyone. Most transient alerts just need "for 5 minutes" appended.
3. **Set a page budget and treat breaches as work.** Something like: more than two pages in a night, or more than five in a week, and the top source becomes a ticket that gets prioritized like a feature. Without this the cleanup happens once and the noise grows back.
4. **Make sure a night on-call actually costs the schedule something.** A person who was up at 3am is not doing useful work the next day. If they're still expected to hit sprint commitments, the burnout is structural and no amount of alert tuning fixes it.

## The scheduling changes, if you still need them

Two worth considering after the above, and they trade against each other:

- **Split day and night rotations.** Nights get fewer people, or a smaller and stricter alert set. Better sleep protection, but it concentrates the pain and needs the night set to be genuinely short.
- **Shorter shifts, two or three days instead of a week.** More handoffs, but nobody is bracing for seven consecutive nights. This is my preference at six people, because the dread is usually about the week ahead more than the pages themselves.

## What I'd do

Steps 1 and 2 this week, step 3 next week, and hold the rotation shape until you've seen a month of the quieter numbers. Then ask the team again. There's a decent chance the schedule stops being the complaint.

One thing that's yours to decide, and it's the uncomfortable one: if bucket one is large, you don't have an on-call problem, you have a reliability problem, and the fix is engineering time against the top three page sources rather than anything in this list. Those are different budgets and different conversations with whoever holds the roadmap.

1% free-to-paid is roughly the middle of the range for self-serve freemium, so before diagnosing it, check whether it's actually broken. Widely cited benchmarks put self-serve freemium somewhere around 1 to 5%, and the spread inside that band is mostly about product category and price point, not about which team is better. If you're at 1% and growing the top of the funnel, that might be a working business.

I don't know your numbers, so I can't tell you which it is. Here's how to find out in about a day of querying.

## Split the funnel first

The single measurement that separates the two diagnoses:

**Of users who genuinely activated (used the core feature enough to get the value), what fraction converted?**

- **Activated users convert at a normal or high rate, but few users activate.** Product problem. People aren't reaching the point where paying makes sense. Your 1% is an onboarding and activation number wearing a pricing costume.
- **Lots of users activate, use the product repeatedly, and don't convert.** Pricing or packaging problem. They got the value and decided it wasn't worth the money, or the paid tier doesn't contain anything they need.

You need a real activation definition to run this, not "signed up and clicked around." Pick the action that correlates with retention at week four and use that.

## Then check three more things

1. **Do free users hit the limit?** If most never touch the ceiling of the free tier, the free tier is too generous and this is packaging. If they hit it and churn instead of paying, it's price or value.
2. **What's the retention curve for free users who never pay?** People who stay free for months and keep using it are getting the job done for free. That's a packaging problem with a clear fix. People who leave in week one never got far enough to have an opinion about your price, which is activation.
3. **Where do they abandon on the paid path?** If they reach the pricing page and leave, that's price or plan clarity. If they start checkout and drop, that's often something dull like payment methods or a required annual commitment.

## My read on how to sequence it

Run the activation split first, because it's one query and it rules out half the possible work. Then look at limit-hitting. Those two together get you to the right diagnosis in most cases without talking to anyone.

After that, talk to fifteen activated non-converters. Not a survey; fifteen calls. The pattern shows up fast and it's the only method that tells you *why*, which neither of the numbers above can.

Do not raise or lower price as the first experiment. It's the most visible lever and the least informative, because it changes the answer you're trying to measure while you're measuring it.

Talk to the rest of the team before you talk about backfilling. The rattle is not about workload, it's people asking themselves whether the leaver knows something they don't, and that question gets louder every day you leave it unaddressed.

## This week, in order

1. **Get the real reason from the leaver, privately, today or tomorrow.** Not the exit interview version. Ask what would have had to be different, and ask early enough that they're still emotionally in the building. If the answer names something fixable and shared, you have a retention problem and not a departure, and the rest of this week changes.
2. **Tell the team yourself, before the leaver does, and before the rumor.** Short, factual, no spin. They're leaving, when their last day is, that you're sorry to see them go, that you're figuring out coverage and will say more within a week. Do not announce a backfill plan you don't have.
3. **Have a 1:1 with each remaining person within 48 hours of that.** These are the ones that matter. Ask directly how they're doing and whether they're thinking about it too. You'll get one or two honest answers, and those tell you whether this is one departure or the first of three.
4. **Say out loud who is not picking up the extra work.** The reflex is for the most conscientious person to absorb it silently, and that's often the same person who leaves next. Name what's getting dropped instead. Something has to be, and deciding it beats letting it be discovered.
5. **Start the knowledge transfer with a written list, not a meeting series.** Have the leaver write down what they own, what only they know, and what's on fire. One document, an hour of their time. Meetings for the top three items only.

## What not to do

**Don't counteroffer**, unless the reason in step 1 is something you can genuinely fix and would have fixed anyway. Counteroffers mostly buy a few months and teach the team that leverage comes from resigning.

**Don't get loudly positive about it.** "Great opportunity for growth" lands as management noise and costs you credibility for the harder conversations in step 3.

**Don't rush the backfill decision.** A departure is one of the few moments you can reshape a team without a reorg, and the shape you had was designed for a person who's leaving. You have a few weeks. Use one of them to think.

## The call that's yours

Whether this is a signal or an event. One strong engineer leaving for a bigger job is an event. One strong engineer leaving and two others hesitating in their 1:1s is a signal, and the correct response is to fix whatever they name rather than to hire. Step 3 is what tells you which one you're in, which is why it's the step to protect if the week gets busy.

A 504 tells you which hop gave up, and almost nothing about why. It's a location marker, not a diagnosis.

Specifically: something acting as a proxy (load balancer, API gateway, CDN, reverse proxy, service mesh sidecar) sent a request upstream and did not get a complete response before its own timeout expired. The proxy generated that 504 itself. Your application almost certainly never produced it, and in most cases never even knows the client is gone.

## What it rules in and out

- **The request reached the proxy.** DNS, TLS, routing, and network path to that hop all worked. A 504 is proof of connectivity, which is more than a connection error gives you.
- **The upstream was reachable but slow, or accepted the connection and went quiet.** If the upstream had refused the connection or been unreachable, you'd typically get a 502 or a 503 instead. Slow versus dead is the practical distinction between 504 and 502.
- **It says nothing about which upstream.** In a chain of `CDN -> load balancer -> gateway -> service -> database`, any link can be the slow one and every proxy in front of it can report a 504. The one you see is just the outermost impatient hop.

## How to find the actual hop

1. **Find the timeout value that fired.** If the 504 came back at almost exactly 30 or 60 seconds, that's a configured timeout and it names the proxy. The number tells you which config to read.
2. **Check whether the upstream logged the request at all.** If the application has no log line for it, the request died before reaching it, and the problem is between the proxy and the app: connection pool exhaustion, no healthy backends, a queue. If the app *does* have a log line and the app's own duration exceeds the proxy timeout, the app is genuinely slow and you now have something to profile.
3. **Compare the app's completion time to the proxy's timeout.** Requests that complete at 45 seconds behind a 30-second proxy timeout are doing the work and throwing it away. That's the most common shape of this, and it's usually one slow query or one unbounded external call.
4. **Check whether it's all requests or one route.** All routes means capacity, saturation, or a shared dependency. One route means that route's work.

## The trap

Raising the proxy timeout makes the 504 go away and makes the user experience worse, because now they wait 90 seconds for the same failure. Only raise it when you've confirmed the work legitimately takes that long and there's no way to make it asynchronous. Otherwise you've hidden the signal and kept the problem.

Expand and contract, with a batched backfill. Don't attempt a single `ALTER TABLE` on 200GB, and don't reach for a full logical replication cutover unless the schema change is drastic enough that expand-contract can't express it.

The shape: add the new structure alongside the old, write to both, backfill the history in chunks, switch reads, then drop the old. Every step is individually reversible, which is the entire point at this size.

## The sequence

1. **Add the new columns or table, nullable, no default that rewrites rows.** On Postgres 11 and later, adding a column with a constant default is metadata-only and fast, but a volatile default or a type change is a full rewrite. Check which one you're doing before you run it.
2. **Deploy code that writes both old and new.** Application-level dual write is easier to reason about; a trigger is fewer deploys but harder to debug and it taxes every write. I'd take the application dual write unless you have writers you don't control.
3. **Backfill in batches**, ordered by primary key, a few thousand rows per transaction, with a short sleep between batches. Track progress in a small table so it's resumable, because it will get interrupted. Watch replication lag while it runs and slow down if it grows; a backfill that outruns your replicas is how this turns into an outage.
4. **Verify before you trust it.** Count both sides, then checksum a sample of rows, then check the edges: nulls, the oldest rows, anything written during the backfill window. The rows written concurrently with the backfill are where the bugs live.
5. **Add the constraints and indexes you deferred**, using `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `NOT VALID` constraints followed by `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`. Both avoid the long exclusive locks that the plain forms take.
6. **Switch reads to the new structure**, behind a flag so you can flip back in seconds rather than a deploy.
7. **Wait.** Days, not hours. Then stop the dual write, then drop the old columns. This is the step everyone wants to compress and it's the only one that's free to leave alone.

## The parts that actually bite

**Lock waits, not lock duration.** Even a metadata-only `ALTER` needs an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, and if a long-running query holds a conflicting lock, your `ALTER` queues behind it *and everything else queues behind your `ALTER`*. Set `lock_timeout` to something like `3s` on every DDL statement and retry. Without this, one instant migration takes the table down for the length of somebody's analytics query.

**Bloat and autovacuum.** Backfilling 200GB of updates writes a new row version for every row touched. Disk usage can roughly double, and autovacuum needs to keep up. Confirm you have the headroom before you start, not at 70% through.

**Foreign keys and triggers on the table** will fire during the backfill and can multiply its cost by a lot. Check what's attached before estimating.

## When to use logical replication instead

If the transformation can't be expressed as "old columns plus new columns in the same table," for instance you're splitting one table into three with different keys, then set up a second table or database, replicate into it with a transformation, and cut over. It's more infrastructure and a real cutover moment, but it keeps the transformation logic in one place instead of scattered across dual-write paths.

## My call

Expand-contract for anything short of a structural split. It's slower in calendar time and it's the one where every intermediate state is a working system, which at 200GB is what you're buying. Budget days for the backfill, not an evening.

One decision that's yours: whether you can tolerate the dual-write period at all from a correctness standpoint. If some writer bypasses your application layer, dual write in the app is a lie and you need triggers. Worth checking what has credentials to that table before step 2.
